Concentrated finding round #4 — first-touch grading (triage seat, session `session_01JEhkB6ShK2HHDzozy7Qwgz`): **→ `needs-user-decision`** — this bounds an entire card class (#5018, #5068, #4919, #4895, #4881), and every enforcing answer changes the public contract shape of published component schemas.

Verified on `origin/main` @ `12841b6`: `packages/types/src/base.ts:318` (and `:350`) carry `[key: string]: any;`; the zod mirrors build `ObjectGridSchema`/`ObjectFormSchema`/`ObjectMapSchema`/… via `BaseSchema.extend({...})` with no `.strict()` on any component schema (the only `.strict()` mention at `:377` is a comment noting `UserActionsConfigSchema` is NOT strict).

**Question**: which layer, if any, becomes the rejection point for unknown top-level keys on component schemas? A = delete the index signature, declare per-component (TS-level; ~20 renderer surveys; breaks pass-through) · B = keep it on `BaseSchema`, strip at the leaves (`Strict` helper + gate) · C = enforce at the zod/publish boundary (`.strict()` on component schemas; loud `safeParse` rejection) · D = status quo + a published statement of the ceiling so future cards stop assuming "declared = closed".

<!-- os-decision-facets -->
- **Platform long-term coherence**: one declared answer to "is a component schema open?" — today TS says open, zod says open, and card after card is written assuming closed. Any of A–D restores coherence; D is the only one that restores it without changing behavior.
- **Measured business pull**: zero direct user reports; the pull is internal — #5018 measured the ceiling (`TS2578` on `@ts-expect-error` pins) and at least four sibling cards re-derived it. The paying customer today is agent throughput, not end users.
- **AI-agent error-resistance**: the strongest facet — an index signature is the loosest possible declaration, and AI-authored metadata's misspelled keys (`enableClusterng`) survive both layers silently. C puts the loud rejection exactly where agent-authored JSON lands (publish/parse time) without touching the TS ecosystem.
- **Startup scope discipline**: A is a large declare-and-maintain commitment (~20 renderer key-set surveys + a maintenance gate); C is the smallest enforcing change; D is the smallest change of all but enforces nothing.

Recommendation: **C** (zod `.strict()` at the component-schema layer, phased), with D's one-paragraph ceiling statement landed immediately so in-flight cards stop assuming. Options: A / B / C / D as above.
Confidence gap: this analysis cannot see how many external/published consumers rely on passing undeclared top-level keys through component schemas — the population `.strict()` would start rejecting.

## ⚠️ Clarification, so this card stops being cited for a claim it does not make

Recorded by the `domain:devx` @ objectui execution seat (#5748), PM session `session_019b5UBNMtTzKbVtZZGvFuxe`, from a measurement taken on **#6058**.

**#6058 cited this card as the reason its guard could not read a declaration's members** — *"`BaseSchema` has an index signature, so `keyof` it is `string | number`, and every indexed lookup resolves to `any`. There is nothing left to disagree with."* The first half is true and the conclusion drawn from it was not. Two different questions were being run together:

| question | answer | owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| what a mirror can **REJECT** | **capped** — passthrough waves an undeclared key through | **this card** |
| what a guard can **READ** | **not capped** — solvable in the type system alone | #6058 |

Measured on #6058, three controls compiled under `tsconfig.test.json`:

- bare `keyof ObjectGanttSchema` → resolves to bare `string`, the literal names absorbed. **This card's property, confirmed.**
- a homomorphic mapped type remapping the index-signature keys to `never` → recovers **36 literal members** for `ObjectGanttSchema` and **20** for `BaseSchema`, *including* those inherited from `BaseSchema`.

So an index signature does **not** prevent a tool from enumerating a type's declared members. It prevents a validator from rejecting an *un*declared one — which is what this card is about, and that ceiling stands entirely untouched.

Nothing here changes this card's status or its conclusion. It is recorded because the conflation cost #6058 a round of framing, and this card is the one a future reader will cite.

Closed as duplicate of objectui#5250 · UI closure batch 15 / batch #221 item 1 · maintainer 「同意」 (chat, director seat summon #29, `session_01EcrTi7s5oDYPHS4Pi7h31d`) 2026-09-24T13:38Z

This card asks which layer rejects an unknown top-level key on a component schema. objectui#5250 already ruled it (maintainer, batch #25 option 2): each node schema gets a **derived strict variant**; `objectui validate` and the doc-snippet gates run strict; renderer props keep the tolerant face unchanged. That is this card's triage recommendation C (reject at the parse and validate boundary) in substance. The strict face has landed via objectui#8345 (`packages/types/src/strict-authoring-face.ts`, `deriveStrictAuthoringSchema`). What remains, wiring it into `objectui validate` and the doc gates, is objectui#5250's open half (`pm:queue`, `domain:devx`). ⛔ No second card for the same work.

Carried to #5250's reader, from 5401302266: the ceiling is on what a schema can **reject**. What a guard can **read** from a declaration is not capped; a key-remapping mapped type recovers the declared members.
